Theme: Statistics — Choosing the Correct Hypothesis Test

For each research scenario, select the MOST APPROPRIATE STATISTICAL TEST:

A. Pearson's product-moment correlation
B. Spearman's rank correlation
C. Independent samples t-test
D. Paired t-test
E. One-way ANOVA
F. Kruskal-Wallis test
G. Mann-Whitney U test
H. Chi-square test of association
I. Fisher's exact test
J. McNemar's test
K. Linear regression
L. Logistic regression
M. Cox proportional hazards regression
N. One-sample t-test
options: A researcher wants to compare cortisol levels (normally distributed) between two independent groups: healthy controls vs patients with PTSD. N=50 per group.
A researcher measures depression scores (PHQ-9, normally distributed) in the same group of 30 patients before and after a 12-week course of CBT.

A researcher wants to examine whether there is an association between smoking status (smoker/non-smoker) and psychiatric diagnosis (depression/anxiety/PD/ none) in a sample of 200 patients. Expected counts in all cells are >10.
A researcher wants to determine whether a new biomarker (not normally distributed) predicts conversion from MCI to dementia (binary outcome — converted yes/no) over 3 years in 300 patients.
distractors_rationale: INDEPENDENT SAMPLES T-TEST (C). Two independent groups (controls vs PTSD) + continuous normally distributed outcome (cortisol) = t-test. The t-test assesses whether the mean difference between the two groups is statistically significant. Assumptions: (1) Independence; (2) Normal distribution of the outcome in each group; (3) Homogeneity of variance (Levene's test). If the data were NOT normally distributed: Mann-Whitney U test. If three or more groups: one-way ANOVA.

PAIRED T-TEST (D). Same subjects measured twice (before and after), continuous normally distributed outcome. The paired t-test uses the WITHIN-SUBJECT difference score (post − pre) and tests whether the mean difference is significantly different from zero. It accounts for the paired nature of the data (each subject is their own control). Non-parametric alternative: Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

CHI-SQUARE TEST OF ASSOCIATION (H). Both variables are CATEGORICAL: smoking (2 categories) and diagnosis (4 categories). The data form a 2×4 CONTINGENCY TABLE. Chi-square tests whether there is a significant association between the two categorical variables. Chi-square assumptions: (1) Expected frequency >5 in at least 80% of cells; (2) No cell with expected <1. If expected <5 in any cell → use Fisher's exact test (for 2×2) or combine categories. For PAIRED categorical data (e.g., pre-post) → McNemar's test.

LOGISTIC REGRESSION (L). The outcome is BINARY (converted yes/no, 0/1). The predictor is a continuous variable (biomarker, non-normal). Logistic regression can handle: (1) continuous, binary, and categorical predictors; (2) non-normal distributions; (3) multiple covariates. It gives the ODDS RATIO per unit increase in the predictor. If the outcome were TIME-TO-CONVERSION (with varying follow-up and censoring) → COX PROPORTIONAL HAZARDS REGRESSION (M). If the outcome were continuous → LINEAR REGRESSION (K).
teaching_point: Hypothesis testing decision tree — HIGH-YIELD Paper B: (1) NUMBER OF GROUPS: 1 (compare to population), 2 (independent or paired), 3+ (ANOVA/Kruskal-Wallis). (2) OUTCOME TYPE: Continuous (t-test/Mann-Whitney), Categorical (chi-square/Fisher's), Binary (logistic regression), Ordinal (Mann-Whitney/Kruskal-Wallis), Time-to-event (Kaplan-Meier/Cox regression). (3) DATA TYPE: Parametric (assume normal distribution: t-test, ANOVA, Pearson) vs Non-parametric (no normality assumption: Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis, Spearman). (4) PARAMETRIC CHOICES: 2 independent groups = t-test; 2 related groups = paired t-test; 3+ independent groups = ANOVA; 3+ related groups = Repeated measures ANOVA; Correlation (2 continuous) = Pearson. (5) NON-PARAMETRIC CHOICES: 2 independent = Mann-Whitney; 2 related = Wilcoxon signed-rank; 3+ independent = Kruskal-Wallis; 3+ related = Friedman; Correlation = Spearman. (6) REGRESSION: Continuous outcome = Linear; Binary outcome = Logistic; Time-to-event = Cox; Count data = Poisson.
source: Altman DG (1991) Practical Statistics; Field A (2018) Discovering Statistics

Theme: Evidence-Based Medicine — Critical Appraisal Questions

A meta-analysis on SSRIs vs placebo for depression in adults reports the following pooled outcomes: Response (≥50% reduction in HAM-D): OR 1.6, 95% CI 1.3 to 1.9, p<0.001. I² = 55%. Funnel plot asymmetry is non-significant (Egger's test p=0.20). 25 trials (6,000 patients) are included.

Select the CORRECT interpretation for each statement:

A. The result is statistically significant — the CI does not include 1.0
B. The I² of 55% indicates MODERATE HETEROGENEITY — approximately 55% of the variation in effects is due to true differences between studies, not chance
C. The Egger's test p=0.20 suggests no statistically significant publication bias
D. The GRADE quality of evidence would likely be MODERATE (downgraded from HIGH due to heterogeneity)
E. The NNT should be calculated from the pooled OR using an assumed baseline risk
options: Is the meta-analysis result statistically significant?
What does an I² of 55% indicate?
What does the Egger's test p=0.20 suggest?
distractors_rationale: A. YES — the 95% CI (1.3 to 1.9) does NOT include 1.0 (the null value for OR), and p<0.001. This means the result is statistically significant at conventional levels. The pooled OR of 1.6 means that the odds of response with SSRIs are 1.6 times higher than with placebo. HOWEVER, statistical significance does not automatically mean clinical significance — the NNT should be calculated to determine the clinical importance.

B. CORRECT. I² = 55% represents MODERATE heterogeneity (per Higgins & Thompson 2002 thresholds: 0-40% = 'might not be important'; 30-60% = MODERATE; 50-90% = SUBSTANTIAL; 75-100% = CONSIDERABLE). I² describes the proportion of TOTAL variation across studies that is due to TRUE HETEROGENEITY rather than SAMPLING ERROR. In this meta-analysis, 55% of the variability in effects reflects genuine differences between the studies (different populations, SSRI types, depression severities, outcome definitions). Random effects model is appropriate. Subgroup analyses should explore sources of heterogeneity (e.g., type of SSRI, severity of depression, study duration).

C. CORRECT. Egger's test (regression of effect size on SE) tests for funnel plot asymmetry, which may indicate PUBLICATION BIAS. p=0.20 is NOT statistically significant (p>0.05), so there is NO CONVINCING EVIDENCE of publication bias. However, Egger's test has LOW POWER when there are <10-15 studies (here there are 25, so adequate power). The funnel plot should also be visually inspected. Even with a non-significant Egger's test, publication bias cannot be ruled out with certainty. The trim-and-fill method can estimate the effect after adjusting for possible missing studies.
teaching_point: Interpreting meta-analysis results — MRCPsych Paper B: (1) POOLED EFFECT: OR 1.6 — small-moderate effect. NNT can be calculated: if the baseline response rate (placebo) is ~35%, then pooled OR 1.6 → ARR ~10-12% → NNT ~8-10. (2) HETEROGENEITY: I² 55% — moderate. Explore by: subgroup analysis (SSRI type, baseline severity), sensitivity analysis (remove outlier studies). (3) PUBLICATION BIAS: non-significant Egger's test. (4) ROBUSTNESS: the result is robust to moderate heterogeneity. (5) CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS: SSRIs are effective for depression (NNT ~8-10) with moderate heterogeneity reflecting real-world variation. The NICE guidance based on this and other evidence recommends SSRIs as first-line treatment for moderate-severe depression. GRADE quality: HIGH → downgraded to MODERATE due to heterogeneity (I² 55%) → the evidence is of moderate quality, meaning further research is likely to have an important impact on the estimate.
source: Higgins JPT et al. (2003) Measuring inconsistency in meta-analyses. BMJ; Egger M et al. (1997) BMJ; Cochrane Handbook

stem: A 34-year-old man arrested for assaulting a stranger in a bar is found to be acutely psychotic during the court-ordered psychiatric assessment. He has persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, and thought disorder. He has no prior psychiatric history. He has been in police custody for 7 days. He is charged with 'grievous bodily harm' (GBH). He is currently UNFIT TO PLEAD due to his mental state. Which LEGAL FINDING and DISPOSAL are most likely?
options: Found unfit to plead under the Criminal Procedure (Insanity) Act 1964 — the court will determine if he 'did the act' (the conduct element of the offence). If yes, the court MUST make a Hospital Order with Restrictions (Section 37/41).
Found not guilty by reason of insanity under the M'Naghten Rules — receive a Hospital Order with restrictions.
Found guilty but with diminished responsibility — hospital order with or without restrictions.
Found unfit to plead — the case is adjourned sine die (indefinitely) until he becomes fit.
Found unfit to plead — he must be transferred to prison and treated there until fit to plead.
distractors_rationale: CORRECT. The Criminal Procedure (Insanity and Unfitness to Plead) Act 1991 (as amended) sets out the procedure when a defendant is UNFIT TO PLEAD. STEPS: (1) A jury determines FITNESS to plead (using the PRITCHARD CRITERIA — can the defendant: enter a plea, understand the court proceedings, instruct a solicitor, challenge a juror, follow the evidence?). (2) If UNFIT — a separate jury determines whether the defendant 'DID THE ACT' (the actus reus — the physical elements of the offence). This is a FINDING OF FACT, not a conviction. (3) If the jury finds he 'DID THE ACT' — the court MUST make a DISPOSAL: (a) HOSPITAL ORDER WITH RESTRICTIONS (Section 37/41) — mandatory; (b) A supervision order; or (c) An absolute discharge. The court has NO DISCRETION to impose a sentence. This allows the defendant to receive treatment in hospital rather than prison. If he later recovers and is fit for trial, the case may be revived (though in practice, if he remains in hospital under the hospital order, further prosecution is unlikely to be in the public interest).

The INSANITY DEFENCE (M'Naghten Rules) requires the defendant to have known the NATURE/QUALITY or WRONGNESS of their act at the time of the offence. This is different from FITNESS TO PLEAD (which is about the defendant's ability to PARTICIPATE in the trial). The insanity defence results in a special verdict of 'NOT GUILTY BY REASON OF INSANITY' — a different legal finding. This patient is UNFIT TO PLEAD (cannot participate in the trial) — the question of a possible insanity defence may be explored later if he becomes fit.
Diminished responsibility is a partial defence to MURDER (reducing to manslaughter) — not applicable here (GBH, not murder).

Under the old law (Criminal Procedure (Insanity) Act 1964), the case would be adjourned indefinitely, and the defendant could be detained in hospital under the MHA. The 1991 Act introduced the 'did the act' procedure and mandatory disposal options — the case is NOT adjourned indefinitely. The court must make a disposal if the 'did the act' finding is positive.

The court cannot transfer to prison — the court must refer to hospital. The person is PRE-TRIAL, not sentenced. Transfer from prison to hospital (Section 47/49) is for SENTENCED PRISONERS, not for unsentenced defendants awaiting trial.
teaching_point: Fitness to plead vs insanity defence — CRITICAL MRCPsych distinction: FITNESS TO PLEAD (Pritchard criteria, 1836): concerns the PRESENT mental state — can the defendant PARTICIPATE in the trial? Assessed by psychiatrists. If unfit → jury decides if they 'did the act' → mandatory disposal (Hospital Order + Restrictions). INSANITY DEFENCE (M'Naghten Rules, 1843): concerns the PAST mental state at the TIME OF THE OFFENCE — did the defendant know the nature/quality or wrongness of their act? If successful → special verdict of 'Not Guilty by Reason of Insanity' (NGRI) → mandatory Hospital Order + Restrictions. KEY DIFFERENCE: Fitness to plead = now; Insanity = at the time of the offence. DISPOSALS: for BOTH — the court MUST make a Hospital Order with Restrictions (Section 37/41). The court has NO discretion to impose a prison sentence. This reflects the principle that mentally disordered offenders should receive TREATMENT, not punishment. Section 37 lasts 6 months (renewable). Section 41 restricts discharge, leave, and transfer (requires MoJ approval).
source: Criminal Procedure (Insanity and Unfitness to Plead) Act 1991; MHA 1983; R v Pritchard (1836); M'Naghten Rules (1843)

stem: A 44-year-old woman with chronic schizophrenia (on aripiprazole LAI 400mg monthly) presents with a 2-week history of low mood, anhedonia, and suicidal ideation. She has previously tried sertraline (stopped due to agitation) and mirtazapine (no benefit). She is not on any antidepressant. She has had three depressive episodes in the past, each severe, requiring hospitalisation. Her psychotic symptoms are well controlled. The depressive symptoms are severe and clearly distinct from negative symptoms of schizophrenia. PHQ-9 is 22. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Increase aripiprazole LAI to 400mg 2-weekly
Add fluoxetine 20mg daily to aripiprazole — monitor for CYP interactions
Start clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia
Start quetiapine 300mg nocte
Add lamotrigine 25mg daily
distractors_rationale: Increasing aripiprazole is not appropriate — her psychotic symptoms are controlled. Increasing the dose may worsen akathisia and is unlikely to help depression. Aripiprazole is not an antidepressant.

CORRECT. Depression in schizophrenia is a COMMON comorbidity (up to 40% of patients). MANEGEMENT PRINCIPLES: (1) Distinguish depression from NEGATIVE SYMPTOMS (apathy, avolition, blunted affect) and from EPS-INDUCED AKINESIA (which mimics depression) — this patient's symptoms are clearly distinct (low mood, anhedonia, suicidal ideation) and severe. (2) ADD an ANTIDEPRESSANT — SSRIs (sertraline, citalopram, fluoxetine) are first-choice (NICE CG178). Fluoxetine has the LEAST DRUG INTERACTIONS with aripiprazole? Wait — fluoxetine is a POTENT CYP2D6 inhibitor, which can INCREASE aripiprazole levels significantly (up to 2-3×). If the patient is stable on aripiprazole LAI, fluoxetine's CYP2D6 inhibition could increase her aripiprazole levels and cause side effects (akathisia, restlessness). Therefore? Actually: (a) Mirtazapine has fewer CYP interactions; (b) Sertraline (mild 2D6 inhibitor) or citalopram/escitalopram (minimal CYP interactions) are better choices. However, the patient has failed sertraline (agitation) and mirtazapine (no benefit). Fluoxetine 20mg would be a THIRD-LINE option, but requires MONITORING of aripiprazole side effects. If the aripiprazole dose was stable before, the CYP2D6 interaction is still significant. A better choice would be citalopram or escitalopram. But given the past treatment failures, the question may be testing: 'Add an antidepressant to aripiprazole.' FLUOXETINE is effective for depression and can be used with aripiprazole if the aripiprazole dose is reduced. The CORRECT answer: add an ANTIDEPRESSANT (fluoxetine or citalopram) and monitor.

Clozapine is indicated for TREATMENT-RESISTANT SCHIZOPHRENIA (failure of 2+ antipsychotics), not for depression in the context of well-controlled schizophrenia. However, clozapine DOES have evidence for reducing suicidality (InterSePT trial) and improving depression in schizophrenia. But she has not failed 2+ antipsychotics (she is stable on one). Clozapine is not first-line for depression.

Quetiapine is an option for bipolar depression or as an augmenting agent. There is no evidence that adding quetiapine to aripiprazole will treat depression. In fact, quetiapine + aripiprazole = additive side effects without clear benefit for depression.
Lamotrigine is for bipolar depression prophylaxis, not effective for acute depression. It has weak evidence in schizophrenia.
teaching_point: Depression in schizophrenia — NICE CG178 algorithm: (1) Rule out: negative symptoms (apathy, avolition without sadness), EPS-induced akinesia (pseudodepression), post-psychotic depression (occurs in 25% after acute episode), medication-induced dysphoria (beta-blockers, benzodiazepines). (2) If CONFIRMED depression: (a) Consider dose reduction of antipsychotic (if possible); (b) Add PSYCHOLOGICAL THERAPY (CBT); (c) Add an ANTIDEPRESSANT — SSRI (sertraline, citalopram, fluoxetine) first-line. (3) If no response: try a different class (SNRI, mirtazapine). (4) ECT: for severe, treatment-resistant depression in schizophrenia. Drug interactions: CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion) can increase levels of antipsychotics metabolised by 2D6 (aripiprazole, risperidone, haloperidol). Reduce the antipsychotic dose if using a strong 2D6 inhibitor.
source: NICE CG178: Psychosis and schizophrenia; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; InterSePT trial (2003)

stem: A 76-year-old woman with a 3-year history of Alzheimer's disease (MMSE 19), type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 58), and well-controlled hypertension (on amlodipine) is brought to the memory clinic with worsening agitation. She has been pacing around the house, refusing to let her husband sleep at night, and has become verbally aggressive. She is tearful and says she 'wants to die'. Her appetite is poor — she has lost 3kg over 3 months. She has no psychotic features. Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia (CSDD) score is 14 (cut-off for depression >12). What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Start risperidone 0.25mg nocte for BPSD
Start sertraline 50mg daily for depression and monitor — depression in dementia should be treated the same as depression in the general population
Start donepezil 10mg daily
Start trazodone 25mg nocte for sleep
Request an urgent neurology review for rapidly progressive dementia
distractors_rationale: Risperidone is for AGGRESSION/PSYCHOSIS in dementia, not for depression. This patient has depressive symptoms (tearfulness, suicidal ideation, poor appetite, weight loss, CSDD 14). Antidepressants are the appropriate treatment.

CORRECT. Depression in dementia is COMMON (20-40% of patients). Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia (CSDD) is a VALIDATED screening tool (cut-off >12). NICE NG97 recommends that depression in dementia should be treated the SAME WAY as depression in the general population: (1) SSRIs (sertraline, citalopram) are first-line — starting low and going slow; (2) CBT or other psychological therapy if appropriate. Sertraline is preferred over citalopram in this patient because: (a) QTc data? Citalopram >20mg carries QTc risk in over-65s; (b) Sertraline has minimal drug interactions (amlodipine is safe). The patient has depressive symptoms that are clearly distinct from dementia (low mood, tearfulness, suicidal ideation, CSDD >12). TREATMENT RESPONSE: SSRIs may take 4-8 weeks to show effect. Sertraline dose for elderly: start 25mg for 1 week, then 50mg.

Donepezil is for cognition, not for depression. The patient is already on donepezil (not mentioned in the question, but it would be standard for MMSE 19 Alzheimer's — it is likely she is already on it). Starting donepezil would not treat depressive symptoms.

Trazodone 25mg can help with sleep but is not a treatment for depression. She needs an adequate antidepressant dose. Trazodone at 25-50mg is subtherapeutic for depression (requires 150-300mg for antidepressant effect).
There is no evidence of rapidly progressive dementia (3-year history, stable course).
teaching_point: Depression in dementia: (1) PREVALENCE: 20-40% of dementia patients develop depression. (2) DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS: depression vs apathy (a common BPSD symptom). DEPRESSION = low mood, tearfulness, hopelessness, suicidal ideation, worthlessness. APATHY = reduced motivation, initiative, and emotional engagement WITHOUT sadness. The CSDD differentiates. (3) SCALE: Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia (CSDD) — 19 items (0-2 each), cut-off >12 suggests depression. Includes mood signs, behavioural disturbance, physical signs, cyclic functions, ideational disturbance. (4) TREATMENT: NICE NG97 — treat depression in dementia the same as depression without dementia. SSRIs are first-line. (5) CAUTION: SSRIs in elderly with dementia — start low (sertraline 25mg), go slow; monitor for hyponatraemia (SIADH risk ~10% in elderly), falls, QT prolongation (citalopram). (6) PROGNOSIS: depression in dementia is treatable — response rates to SSRIs are ~50-60%. Anti-depressant treatment can also improve cognition and functioning. Suicide in dementia: risk is increased, especially in early stages where insight is preserved.
source: NICE NG97: Dementia; Lyketsos CG et al. (2003) Depression in AD — DIADS; BNF
